introduction_markdown:
**GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD - General Certificate of Education Examination. JUNE 2025, ADVANCED LEVEL. English Language, Paper 2 (0730).**

Answer your questions either exclusively from **PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS)** or from **PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS)**.

**PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS) - Duration: Two and a Quarter Hours.** Instructions to candidates: ANSWER ONE QUESTION FROM EACH SECTION (Section A: Composition, Section B: Prescribed Texts, Section C: Creative Writing). ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you no marks.

**PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS) - Duration: Three Hours.** Instructions to candidates: Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will earn you little or no marks. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you little or no marks.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS) - SECTION B: COMPOSITION (20 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (06 marks); Expression (08 marks); Accuracy (06 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly, and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.enonce_markdown: **c)** Online classes are more effective than face-to-face classes. Do you agree?
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Introduction: the claim, and my position (disagree, with nuance).
2. The advantages of online classes: flexibility, savings, access to knowledge.
3. Why they are not more effective: infrastructure and inequality.
4. The human side of the classroom, practical subjects, discipline.
5. Distraction and cheating at home.
6. A blended solution; conclusion.

**Model composition (514 words)**

Since the closure of schools during the pandemic, online classes have become part of the educational landscape, and some people now claim that they are more effective than face-to-face lessons. I do not entirely agree. In my opinion, online learning is a useful complement, but in present conditions the classroom remains the more effective place to learn.

Admittedly, online classes have real advantages. First, they are flexible: a student can follow a lesson from home, at any time, and can watch a recorded video again and again until a difficult point is clear. Second, they save time and money, since there is no need to travel to school in crowded taxis or to pay for daily meals. Third, they open access to knowledge: a learner in a village can attend a lecture given by a professor in another country, and can find animations and practice tests on the internet. For disciplined and self-motivated students, these facilities are a great help.

However, these advantages are not enough to make online classes more effective, especially in a country like ours. The most obvious problem is infrastructure. Many students have no computer or smartphone, and those who have one often face poor network coverage, expensive data bundles and frequent power cuts. A lesson that is interrupted every few minutes is of little value. In rural areas, thousands of children are simply excluded, so that the inequality between rich and poor learners increases.

Furthermore, learning is more than receiving information; it is a human activity. In a classroom, the teacher sees confusion on a pupil's face and explains again, answers questions at once and corrects mistakes immediately. Students learn from each other through group work, debates and friendly competition. Practical subjects such as chemistry, biology and technical drawing need laboratories and tools, which a screen cannot supply. Moreover, the classroom provides discipline and routine, and it teaches social skills, such as cooperation and respect, which are essential for adult life.

Another weakness of online classes is distraction. At home, a student is tempted by social media, games, films and household chores. Without the teacher's eye, many pupils switch off their cameras, leave the lesson and do something else. Teachers also find it difficult to supervise honesty during online tests, so cheating is easy. As a result, many students who followed lessons online during the pandemic returned to school with serious gaps in their knowledge.

Yet it would be wrong to reject online learning completely. The best solution is a blended approach, in which the classroom remains the foundation and technology provides extra support. Teachers can share notes, videos and exercises online for revision, and in emergencies, such as an epidemic or a long strike, online lessons can keep education alive. For this to succeed, the government should improve electricity and internet coverage, reduce the price of data and train teachers.

In conclusion, online classes are a valuable tool, but they are not yet more effective than face-to-face teaching. Until every learner has reliable equipment and the maturity to work alone, the classroom will remain the heart of education.

**Marking grid (the paper prints the split of the 20 marks)**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 6 | A relevant treatment of the topic as set, a clear introduction, paragraphs that each develop one idea, a logical order and a conclusion |
| Expression | 8 | Varied sentence structures, precise vocabulary, suitable register and tone, good use of linking words, a convincing style |
| Accuracy | 6 | Correct grammar, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Writing fewer than 500 or more than 550 words, or ignoring the topic's exact wording (for example listing points instead of telling a story, or giving only one side when asked 'Do you agree?').
2. A weak plan: a long introduction, paragraphs that repeat one idea, no conclusion; or a pre-prepared composition that does not fit the question (it earns no marks).
3. Answering with personal anecdotes only, without weighing the two kinds of classes: 'Do you agree?' needs arguments on both sides.
